question.prompt: Why does hand stretching limit the sound comparison?

options.text: elastic bands cannot vibrate by hand
The applied tension may differ between groups
it changes every box into a different shape

question.explanation: One group pulls harder and no group measures tension. Unequal tension introduces another possible contributor to pitch differences.

stimulus.title: A fictional sound experiment
stimulus.body:
In a classroom model, three groups investigated how the length of a stretched elastic band related to its sound. They used bands of the same kind and plucked them over identical empty boxes. Each group shortened its band gradually and described the pitch it heard.

All three groups reported higher pitches at shorter lengths. However, the bands were stretched by hand. One group pulled much harder than another, and none measured tension. Their descriptions of pitch were also based on listening rather than a recording device.

The class wrote a cautious conclusion: 'Under our test conditions, shorter lengths were associated with higher perceived pitch.' They did not write that length alone had been proved to cause every change. For a new trial, they planned a frame that could hold tension more consistently. They would keep the boxes and band material the same. Their aim was to reduce one uncertainty at a time, not to pretend the first trial had taught them nothing.

workedSolution: One group pulls harder and no group measures tension.
Unequal tension introduces another possible contributor to pitch differences.
reviewFocus: Independently solve without the key; check each alternative and the stated conditions.
Review originality, vocabulary, difficulty and time for an above-average Year 5/6 learner.

question.prompt: What evidence prompted the Willow Court notice?

options.text: every resident reporting a broken tap
unusually high overnight meter flow on three nights
a confirmed leak in one household

question.explanation: The first quoted sentence identifies the meter readings. The notice then explicitly says the readings do not establish a responsible household or a specific cause.

stimulus.title: Water-meter message
stimulus.body:
Residents of Willow Court received this notice after a fictional maintenance review:

'Your shared water meter showed an unusually high overnight flow on three nights. This does not identify a particular household as responsible. It may indicate a leak, a timer setting or legitimate night-time use. Please check visible taps and appliance timers before Friday. Do not enter another resident's property. Report the time and location of any observation to the building manager.

'A plumber will inspect common pipes on Friday morning. Water will be unavailable from 9 am to 10 am, unless the work finishes early. If a fault is found, the manager will send a separate repair plan. The inspection is not a guarantee that every source of water use will be identified.'

One resident read the notice as an accusation. Another read it as proof that a pipe must be leaking. The manager explained that the readings justified a check, while the cause remained uncertain. The requested observations would help choose the next step without turning a possible explanation into a conclusion.

workedSolution: The first quoted sentence identifies the meter readings.
The notice then explicitly says the readings do not establish a responsible household or a specific cause.

stimulus.title: Two library slogans
stimulus.body:
For its late-opening trial, a library considered two poster slogans. 'More hours, more stories' focused on the extra opportunity to read. 'Still a place for you after school' focused on welcome. Both would accompany the same practical details: Tuesday opening until 7 pm for six weeks, with the final bus leaving the nearby stop at 7:10 pm.

The librarians chose the second slogan for the front door because many pupils waited outside for family members. They retained the first on the reading programme flyer. At the end of six weeks they would count visits, collect comments and decide whether staffing the later hours was sustainable. The slogans described hopes for the trial. Attendance and feedback, rather than the slogans alone, would help judge whether those hopes were realised.

The welcoming wording addresses that audience; transport, permanence and staffing promises are absent.

stimulus.title: The bridge notebook
stimulus.body:
When the old footbridge closed, Sam began recording how people crossed the creek. A cyclist pushed her bicycle through the shallow ford. A man with a walking frame turned back. Three children took the long road past the shops. Sam drew each route in a notebook.

At the planning meeting, he expected the adults to admire his neat map. Instead, the engineer asked which routes people could use after rain. Sam had no answer. His observations all came from sunny afternoons.

The next wet morning he returned with his father. The ford had vanished beneath brown water. On his map, Sam drew a dotted line around it and added the date. He did not erase the earlier routes. At the second meeting, his map was untidier, with notes squeezed into the margins. This time he could explain why the shortest route on paper was not always an available route in practice.

The cyclist uses the ford, so confusing the two would change the observation.
